hints: Focus on the carbon attached to the OH group and count how many other carbon atoms are joined to it.
That OH carbon is joined to three other carbons, which is the definition of a tertiary alcohol.
Now look at the C=O carbon and check if it is at the end of the chain or in the middle joined to two carbons.
walkthrough:
**Classify the alcohol group**

Look at the carbon bearing the $\text{OH}$ group. Count the C-C bonds from that carbon.

In compound X, that carbon is bonded to three methyl-type carbons and one $\text{OH}$: $$\text{R}_3\text{C-OH}$$

**Decide primary, secondary or tertiary**

Remember the rule: primary = 1 carbon attached, secondary = 2 carbons attached, tertiary = 3 carbons attached.

Here there are 3 carbons attached, so it is a tertiary alcohol. Lovely and clear.

**Classify the carbonyl group**

Now look at the $\text{C=O}$ group. An aldehyde has $\text{H-C=O}$ at the end of a chain, while a ketone has $\text{C-C(=O)-C}$ in the middle.

In compound X, the $\text{C=O}$ carbon is joined to two carbons with no H on it, so it is a ketone: $$\text{R-CO-R'}$$

**Combine the two answers**

Tertiary alcohol plus ketone gives the correct row. That is a hydroxy-ketone, sometimes called 3-hydroxy-3-methylbutan-2-one.

options.A: Incorrect. The alcohol is not primary because the C-OH carbon is not $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, and the carbonyl is not an aldehyde because there is no $\text{CHO}$ hydrogen.
options.B: Half right, half wrong. The carbonyl is correctly a ketone, but the alcohol is not primary. Students who miscount the carbons around the C-OH may think it is primary.
options.C: Half right, half wrong. The alcohol is correctly tertiary, but the carbonyl is not an aldehyde. Any $\text{C=O}$ is not automatically an aldehyde, it must have a hydrogen directly on the carbonyl carbon.
options.D: Correct. The C-OH carbon has three alkyl groups attached so it is tertiary, and the C=O carbon has two alkyl groups attached so it is a ketone.
